But books have the power to change our lives and you've given me some great suggestions. So in essence, I ask you to engage in the order of persuasion and many of you did just that. So last week we focused on what I'm sure seems elementary. What do you believe and why do you believe it? It seems so simple and so obvious. But trust me, when I tell you, you would be surprised at the number of folks who do not always feel fully equipped to tell you what they believe and why. And hopefully by now, you are embracing the notion that all facets of life will benefit from persuasion. Yes, I was in a courtroom for a long time. And prosecutors do have to persuade judges and juries. And we have to persuade witnesses to come forward and cooperate or testify. And we have to persuade cops to investigate some matters more fully so we can get from arrests to conviction. And yes, I was in politics for a season. And for sure, you need to persuade voters to vote for you and sometimes convince donors to donate to your campaign. And sometimes you have to persuade colleagues to look at an issue in a different way. But the reality is persuasion is everywhere. Persuasion and opportunities to move others exist from the dinner table to the boardroom, from convincing someone to let you return an item at the store without a receipt. to convincing your boss to give you a promotion. The most difficult attempt at persuasion I have ever engaged in was trying to get one of my kids to clean up her room. And that word, her, should be a hint as to which of the two that was. Parents and grandparents, co-workers, friends, there are limitless opportunities for us to move others to a new way of looking at an old issue or looking at something important to you for the first time. Politically, you've heard me say this a hundred times, but we are living in a 50-50 country. And I do not want to die in a 50-50 country. So someone is going to need to embrace persuasion before we are going to navigate this stalemate. And what we have now seems to be intransigence, and the issues are not intractable, not all of them, but some of the participants seem to be. We saw gridlock on full display this week. If ever there were a time to come together and put differences aside and work for the common good, it would be in the throes of a pandemic with our fellow citizens out of work, fearful of ejection, it would be in the throes of a pandemic with our fellow citizens out of work, fearful of eviction or fearful of otherwise not being able to meet their financial and societal obligations. And let's be clear, people do have very different views on the role of government and spending and the line between personal responsibility and the responsibilities of government. Absolutely 100% people of good conscience disagree on those issues. But this isn't that. This is a pandemic complete with economic consequences that our fellow citizens could not have stopped or mitigated. And quite literally, the country was shut down for a period of time with all of the consequences attended thereto. The entire American family was victimized in a sense. and the entire American family is bearing the brunt of a catastrophe we did not create. Some members of our American family had been hurt mightily. So this is the perfect time to come together and act. But there was no agreement this week in Washington. The need was there, but the result was not. I cannot speak to the effort because I was not in the room when the negotiating took place. But it is illustrative of just how broken the modern political system is. It is not as if one side believed nothing needed to be done and the other side believed something must be done. Those are policy disputes. There is an opportunity to persuade thereto, but that involves a conversation about the scope of government. That was not what we had this week. Both sides agreed something needed to be done. Both sides agreed people will run out of unemployment benefits. Both sides agreed people are being hurt because of factors solely outside of their control. And yet there was no agreement. I do have an opinion on why this occurred, but I am not trying to persuade you that I am right. I am trying to persuade you that we are right. We are right to expect more from this broken political system we are experiencing. And we are right to expect more from a media that is more interested in who won and lost the week politically than who lost their home or lost their job. This country is bigger than its politics. This country is us, even when we disagree. So how do we get out of where we are? We break the gridlock with persuasion, moving one side of that 50-50 stalemate towards consensus, commonality, and compassion for those who are suffering mightily. So what are the building blocks of effective persuasion? You have to know what you believe and why. We covered that. But you have to have a factual basis to support what you believe. If you want to be an expert at persuasion, you will need to be fully versed in the evidence, the facts, the truth as it relates to whatever issue you are interested in. If you are interested in gun control, what are the facts on gun use, legal and otherwise? What are the facts on what the current law is? What are the facts on the causal link between the new law is advocated for and the desired effect? Have you studied the issue? Do you know the reasoning behind the Second Amendment? Have you read the Supreme Court decision in Heller, both the majority and the descending opinions? Have you looked at studies on mass shootings or mass killings or death by firearm? Have you looked at prosecution statistics over the past decade? Are we enforcing current laws? Do we need more laws? What are those new laws advocated for specifically tailored to do? If the issue is convincing your child to go to a college in state for less tuition rather than an out of state school with more debt, what are the facts about the relative schools at play? What are the facts on which majors are best for your child or grandchild and what he or she wants to do in life? What are the facts about debt and how long it will take to pay it off? What are the facts on what value, if any, will accrue to your student If she or he attends the more famous out-of-state school as opposed to the less expensive in-state school, nothing undercuts your efforts at persuasion quite like a lack of evidence or support for the position you espouse. So I know it sounds obvious and it should be. but you would be surprised at the folks I run into that express their opinion or perspective and have zero factual support whatsoever for it. It's a book about how to make your point and be heard. The title doesn't hurt to ask, and it is not a political book. It's not a book telling you what you should or should not believe. It is a book designed to help you effectively communicate whatever it is you do or do not believe. Even if you disagree with me, This book can help you make your points and be persuasive. And this book can help you ask the right questions in the right order and in the most compelling and convincing way. And in this book, I discussed some of the homicide cases I prosecuted and the hurdles we had to overcome to persuade a jury of 12. Of course, I knew the facts of those cases. I prosecuted them. So I had to know the facts of who, what, when, where and how. but I did not stop there and neither should you. To be an effective prosecutor or advocate, you need to know your facts but also anticipate what the defense would be, what the other side will say or do. Defendance and defense attorneys in criminal cases do not have to tell the prosecution what their defense is or even if they have a defense. So if you're a prosecutor, you are literally flying blind on what the defense attorney is going to argue or present. But you should spend a lot of time anticipating what the other side of the argument is. What are the weaknesses in your own case? What are the weaknesses in what you believe? What are your evidentiary gaps? Where are you thin when it comes to the facts? If you want to be an effective communicator, I do think you have to know your own case and you have to effectively anticipate the arguments others will make that are contrary to your position. So you got to know the facts on both sides. What else do you need to be heard and understood and move others closer to your way of thinking? This will seem simple too, but trust me, you will see people get this wrong often in life. You have to know your objective or purpose or what success looks like before you utter your first word. I'm Trey Gaudy and we'll have more coming up.
